meaning: Number of registered men from the tribe of Ephraim and from Manasseh's camp at the first census
description: The number 40,500 appears in Numbers as the result of the census of the tribe of Ephraim at Sinai (Num 1:33). Ephraim, son of Joseph, was the tribe that Jacob prophetically placed before his older brother Manasseh (Gen 48:19–20), and which became the bearer of a special blessing. The same number is found for Manasseh's army in Ephraim's camp (Num 2:19), linking the two tribes of Joseph closely together in the census lists. At the second census (Num 26:37), Ephraim's number had fallen to 32,500, a decline that can be seen in connection with the tribe's disobedience and rebellion in the wilderness. In the camp arrangement, Ephraim led the western grouping which also included Manasseh and Benjamin (Num 2:18–24), underscoring Ephraim's prominent role among Joseph's descendants and his position as leader of one of the four main groups around the tabernacle.

versions.meaning: Number of registered men from the tribe of Ephraim at the first census
versions.description: The number 40,500 appears in Numbers as the result of the census of the tribe of Ephraim at Sinai (Num 1:33). Ephraim, son of Joseph, was the tribe that Jacob prophetically placed before his older brother Manasseh (Gen 48:19–20), and which became the bearer of a special blessing. At the second census (Num 26:37), Ephraim's number had fallen to 32,500, a decline that can be seen in connection with the tribe's disobedience and rebellion in the wilderness. The number 40,500 also appears in relation to the tribe of Benjamin in the camp arrangement (Num 2:23) and to the tribe of Dan (Num 1:39), but the passages given here primarily link it to Ephraim's camp on the west side of the tabernacle. In the camp order, Ephraim led the western grouping that also included Manasseh and Benjamin (Num 2:18–24), which underscores Ephraim's prominent role among Joseph's descendants.

footnotes.text: In Numbers 2:19, 40,500 is given as the number for Manasseh's camp in Ephraim's encampment, while Numbers 2:28 states 41,500 (not 40,500) for the tribe of Asher in Dan's encampment. It is therefore important to distinguish precisely between the numbers of the different tribes in the census lists.

Rabbinic tradition sees Ephraim's decline from 40,500 to 32,500 at the second census as a sign of the consequences of sin, and links this among other things to the episode where Ephraim's descendants left Egypt too early (cf. 1 Chron 7:20–22 and Sanhedrin 92b).

The encampment arrangement in Numbers 2, where the tribes are placed in four groups of three around the tabernacle, reflects a cosmic and liturgical order that symbolizes God's presence in the midst of His people.
